title: Why So Many Men Are Unraveling
text:
Jon Ronson had never really thought about the term masculinity until a strange series of events led him down a rabbit hole involving castles, cage fights, and an actor playing a horse. Host Charlie Warzel talks to Ronson about the disinhibited men who are looking for purpose in all the wrong places.

 Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube 

 The following is a transcript of the episode: 

 Jon Ronson: So I think, beginning with deindustrialization, the death of factories, office life eroding, men realizing that certain privileges they had they don’t quite have the same way anymore—feeling kind of tossed around in a sea of conflicting ideologies about what being a man actually means. Should you be more stoical? Should you be more vulnerable? You know, all of these men’s-health influencers giving these differing, contrasting ideas. And so this is a huge societal shift in many different ways. And I think that’s what’s happening. You’ve got men responding to these changes by bowing out, and then you’ve got these other men who are responding by spiraling.

 Charlie Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain , and today we are headed down a rabbit hole that includes ominous castles, public shaming, YouTube, White House cage fighting, all to answer one of life’s burning questions. Why is it that so many men are unraveling these days? Is this part of a changing economy? Part of a bad job market? Is it fallout from the pandemic? Or, is it part of something bigger? A societal failure of some sort, or an outgrowth of what some people have called the masculinity crisis?

 Now those words, masculinity crisis , can cause some people to roll their eyes. Men, of course, continue to enjoy all kinds of societal privilege, and gender inequities abound. But what is clear, I think, if you spent any time engaging with modern politics and culture, is that over the last few decades there has been a very real, if hard to define, debate over what it means to be a man. Jobs and gender roles—they’ve changed, and culture along with it. Much of it for the better. But that change has also created some uncertainty for the men who have been used to being at the center of every household, every office, every institution, marketing campaign, and political decision. And it’s in that uncertainty that all kinds of voices, pickup artists, politicians, incels on 4chan, Andrew Tate, Jordan Peterson—you name it—they’ve all jumped in to offer these competing visions of masculinity.

 Now, some of this has taken the form of toxic, misogynistic, manosphere bullshit. Some of it is just positive or harmless—“dudes rock” kind of stuff. And so many of these lessons, they end up being taught or absorbed, for better or for worse, in online communities and communicated by people who may or may not have ulterior motives. So what happens to regular men in this bizarre online stew that we’re all in? My guest today, the writer and podcaster Jon Ronson, explores that in his new book, The Castle .

 Ronson, to be clear, isn’t really writing about the manosphere or the high-profile grifters or the wild extremes. Instead, Ronson focuses on ordinary people who tend to find themselves in extraordinary situations. For the past three years, Ronson has been reporting on what happens to men when institutions die, when technology lets a million influencers bloom, and culture changes rapidly. What I find so useful about Ronson’s work is that it is curious and is funny, but it’s not overly ideological.

 The Castle is written partly as a mystery and partly as a work of anthropology. For the last decade, Ronson and I have crossed paths on stories numerous times. Like me, his work is always trying to understand what pushes people to believe strange or awful things, and all the ways that technology warps culture, which in turn warps real human beings. So—are men okay? Has the internet driven us all insane? It turns out this is a very complicated question.

 And Jon Ronson joins me now to talk about it all.

 Warzel: Jon Ronson, welcome to Galaxy Brain .

 Ronson: Charlie, it’s a delight to be here. Thank you.

 Warzel: So your newest book, the reason you are talking to me right now—it’s called The Castle , and you’ve written it in such a propulsive, narrative way. But the story is also unique, I think, in that it found you. So tell me a bit about the castle and how it entered your life in what is clearly an extremely personal way.

 Ronson: Yes. I am asleep, and I wake up, and there’s a series of texts from my son, who was in his mid-20s at the time. And so I read the last text first, and the last text says something like: It’s okay; that was completely fucked, but we got out, and we’re safe now. Or something along those lines.

 Warzel: Every parent wants to hear that.

 Ronson: So I frantically read the other texts. And what I gather is that him and three friends have been invited to a party being held by a stranger that one of them had met on Tinder. So it’s like three hours’ drive outside of New York City, into the Connecticut countryside. And when they turn up, this man’s house is a vast, newly built Gothic castle, which is ostentatious even by Gothic-castle standards. It has way too many turrets.

 And so they tentatively cross the drawbridge over the moat and enter to discover that there is no party. They’ve been lured there for some mysterious other reason. So the castle owner comes out, and they say, “I’m sorry, but where’s the party?” And he said, “No, I’ve invited you here to take part in my reality show.” So they said, “What’s the name of your reality show?” And he said, “It’s called 101 Princesses .” They asked what the core concept of 101 Princesses was, and he said, “I’m the lord. I’m looking for my queen, and I’ve got 101 princesses to choose from.”

 Filming began, and it became very clear, very quickly, that this wasn’t a real reality show. He had another agenda. Anyway, that’s basically where their story ends.

 But I then went to the castle. I was so intrigued by what the hell was going on in there. I went to the castle, and a strange and increasingly ominous cat-and-mouse game begins between me and the castle owner. What I thought was the story was that— This guy is trying to be Hugh Hefner. He’s trying to get his, like, you know, princesses in his castle, like the Playboy Mansion. He’s trying to be Hugh Hefner at what is the worst moment in human history to try and be Hugh Hefner. You can’t lord it over your princesses and your castle like it’s the 1970s anymore.

 Throughout the book, I return to the castle to try and find out what the hell is going on. And what I learned gets increasingly dark and extraordinary. But I also tell this wider story of unraveling men failing to adjust to changing times.

 Warzel: So tell me a little bit. The castle owner’s name, I believe, it’s Chris Mark, right? Is the name of the castle owner. But he is a very particular type of character. Tell me a little bit about him, and what immediately caught your eye about this guy.

 Ronson: Yeah, well he’s the great-grandson of a Gilded Age steel tycoon. That’s where his money comes from. His great-grandfather, Clayton Mark, made a vast amount of money manufacturing steel, and then the money is filtered down from generation to generation. And Chris has used his portion of the money to build this giant castle and try and create this kind of fantasy bubble inside of his castle, where he could be the lord. And he invites all of these women.

 But he doesn’t handle my sudden intrusion into his life very well at all. And by the way, it’s not an intrusion. I told him I was a journalist, and he invited me over. But after I leave the cast, so I start to get these ominous messages from him.

 First, legal threats. Threats that he had a team of investigators investigating everything about my life. And then he told me that he had two murderers on his payroll, called Carlos and Brandon. And if I ever wrote anything negative about the castle, Carlos and Brandon would be very angry, and I didn’t want to make them angry. They’ve only just got out of prison. Clearly this is a difficult situation I’m now in.

 Warzel: Hey, guys—it’s Charlie here. A quick interjection: After we recorded this interview with Jon Ronson, Chris Mark—the central character of the book—spoke with The Guardian and pushed back on some of the assertions in The Castle . He told The Guardian that he’d been presented in “a profoundly misleading manner.” Mark denied deliberately deceiving people into coming to the castle, adding that “the gathering was related to a proposed creative project that also had a genuine charitable purpose.” He added: “I strongly dispute any characterization suggesting that I groomed, conditioned, or manipulated women into sexual activity.” And he denied that the text messages referencing Carlos and Brandon in any way constituted a genuine threat: “I did not intend to instruct anyone to physically harm Jon Ronson.” With all that said, back to the interview.

 Warzel: Was that a moment for you? Because it feels like it in the book, where you haven’t decided to make this your next big project. And yet the amount of protestation from him, the intensity of that—is that the moment when you say, Okay, there’s something real here ? Like, I need to devote a lot more time to this, because clearly anyone who’s willing to speak this way to me—there has to be something bigger than just an eccentric man in a castle here. 

 Ronson: Yeah; there was definitely an element of that. That was also, you know—but also it was kind of frightening to get these threats. And I remember times in the past when I’ve done stories which were genuinely frightening. And on each of those occasions, I realized that doing something that’s completely out of my comfort zone, something I would never do if I wasn’t a journalist, quite often the stories that last for years and years are the stories that I’m most proud of. They’re often the most extraordinary stories. And this one truly turned out to be one of those.

 Warzel: Yeah, that’s exactly where I want to go here. Because the story about Mark becomes this through line that animates this bigger story about—I mean, I guess to put it frankly, it’s: What the hell is going on with men in this era? Right? And there’s this personal element that you refer to a couple of times. In this sort of paralyzing fear in your own life, in your own career, of any kind of stagnation, right? Being a writer when you don’t have the idea; you know, you feel purposeless and useless. Have you felt in your own life a masculinity crisis inside of you, that like allowed you to connect with a lot of the people in this story, in this way? This unraveling feeling. Is that something that’s always kind of been a factor in your life and your work?

 Ronson: Well, I would never have put it in terms of the word masculinity . I don’t think, until I started writing this book, I ever said the word masculinity out loud. That’s how little I identify with masculinity. I discovered a statistic writing the book that 10 percent of people feel the same way I do—that we just don’t identify as strongly masculine or feminine. So we’re really in the minority.

 But this desire for purpose, this need to be productive. I once asked Randy Newman this question: Why do you write songs? And he said, It’s how I judge myself, and how I feel better. And that always stayed with me. Because that’s why I am a writer; it’s how I judge myself and how I feel better. And I thought— That’s relevant . Because, you know, we’re living in a time where there’s 6.7 million American men who aren’t only unemployed; they’re not even looking for work. They’ve just bowed out. And so, you know, if purpose is that important to me, what happens to somebody when purpose vanishes? And that was something I wanted to explore.

 Warzel: I wanted to find it a little more—like, what would you argue is happening to these men, who are not in the workforce? Like, what is happening here?

 Ronson: I think, you know, toward the end of researching this, I came across Émile Durkheim’s work on suicide. And he invented this term called anomie , which is that when society abruptly changes, it turns people haywire. And often that manifests as somebody folding in on themselves, withdrawing from the world. A good example is the fall of the Soviet Union. Even people who hated living under Soviet rule would find themselves, after it fell, sitting on the pavement in despair, with their head in their hands, because society’s rules have changed and they didn’t know what to do. And then, some people respond not by folding in but by lashing out in these unrestrained, disinhibited ways.

 So I think a form of anomie is what has taken over, beginning with deindustrialization, the death of factories, office life eroding, men realizing that certain privileges they had they don’t quite have the same weight anymore—feeling kind of tossed around in a sea of conflicting ideologies about what being a man actually means. Should you be more stoical? Should you be more vulnerable? You know, all of these men’s-health influencers giving these differing, contrasting ideas. And then a lot of men who were in this situation become influencers; they go onto YouTube and become content creators. And so this is a huge societal shift in many different ways. And I think that’s what’s happening. You’ve got men responding to these changes by bowing out, and then you’ve got these other men who are responding by spiraling.

 Warzel: So you do this great job of mapping all this. But there’s a point in the book, and I want to tease this out more, where you acknowledge sort of as you’re as you’re moving on from Mark and the castle to make this a broader subject of the book. You acknowledge that this is a hard thing to talk about, right? Because it can veer into sounding like you’re setting up a misogynistic argument. So I’m curious—like what would you say to somebody who hears the premise of The Castle and just goes, Please, not another book trying to drum up pity for the least-subjugated people on Earth —you know, primarily white men.

 What do you think it is that these books, or the discourse around this issue of men—like, what do you think they haven’t put their finger on yet? What is the dissatisfaction that you see in that genre?

 Ronson: Well, I think a lot of the problem is that people, you know, a lot of the people who approach this subject are ideological. And I’m not. I have no agenda whatsoever. I think we’re living in this sort of—I picture an astronaut getting cut loose from their craft and tumbling into the blackness of space. I think all of these things: the death of institutions, the false promise of YouTube as a kind of post-institution utopia. Where people, you know, where a man can thrive, like a wide-open country where a man can thrive through perseverance and grit as an influencer. But of course, that’s a false promise.

 Personally speaking, the thing that interests me the most is what happens when institutions die. Very often, they die for good reason. However, I think that does something to people’s inner lives—this lack of purpose and so on. And I’m not sure that that has properly been written about in this way. And I think that’s a kind of contribution that this book makes.

 Warzel: You acknowledge in the book that in some ways these institutions have failed, but that what can replace them—in the sense of, you know, YouTube in this case—is sometimes worse. And how much would you say the behaviors of the men in this book—that this problem of despair, resentment, and idleness—is due to that collapse of faith, and also the failure of some of these institutions?

 Ronson: Yeah, I think that’s quite a big part of it. Also, another world I look at in this book is the world of the... it’s a smaller part of the book, but I think a very relevant one. It’s the world of the sort of anti-woke influencer. The kind of man who’ll say, The only reason why I haven’t got ahead in life is because I’m a white man, and now we’re being prejudiced against. And it hurts. And so on. And then I dig in, and so they become anti-woke influencers, and they realize that the more extreme—the more they present themselves in a kind of victim narrative—the more money they make. And so they double down on this.

 And I really dig into that and look at when they have a point, and when they don’t have a point. When they’re, you know, exaggerating or manipulating their stories for this kind of nefarious, anti-woke ideological ends. So that’s another thing that the book looks at.

 I’ve got one small section of the book where I look at doofus men in TV advertising. It used to always be, in the old days, women were the figures of mockery in adverts. And now that’s shifted, and men are the figures of mockery.

 Warzel: What is the reason for that? The shift?

 Ronson: Well, I think partly it just became passé to disparage women in TV ads. Also women control most household-spending habits. And so that’s part of the reason why they stopped making women the sort of butt of the jokes.

 Warzel: Bad business decision.

 Ronson: Yeah, exactly. But then advertising, you know—there’s such a paucity of imagination. They think, Well, we’ll just make somebody else the idiots. If it’s not women, it’s going to have to be men. So I’ve watched a kind of, you know, orgy of male buffoonery to research that part of the book. Men falling off cliffs; men leaving their babies on restaurant conveyor belts; men being terrible at sex, you know. And I actually interviewed one of the actors who plays Doofus in Adverts. It made me laugh. He said he did an ad for—what are the insoles?

 Warzel: Dr. Scholl’s, the foot pads? Yeah.

 Ronson : Yeah; he did an advert for them where he said that he’s walking to work and he puts on a pair of insoles, and they’re so comfortable he starts galloping like a horse. And he had to be a bit doofusy for that. So I pointed out to him that 50 years ago, you had the Marlboro Man being stoical and masculine on a horse, and now he has to be the horse. And he pointed out that, yeah—but who do you identify with more? The doofus or the Marlboro Man? And I have to admit that I identify more with the doofus.

 Warzel: And so it seems like, I mean, is someone listening to this might say, you know, where is the through line there?

 Ronson: There is a through line.

 Warzel: But it’s a kind of a death-by-a-thousand-cuts thing, right? Like, especially if you are someone who feels this subjugation, right? Rightly or wrongly, that if you start looking for it, you can see it in so many different places. And seeing it in so many different places becomes— Okay now, I’m under assault. Now I’m under attack. There are no positive, strong role models. Things like that. There’s no Marlboro Man, whatever. And then it seems, like, to put the institutions and the alternative influencers that come in to take the place of that—that you have these people creating their own versions of that. Of something to aspire to.

 And you have this line that I’d love for you to expound on more. Where you say: “As institutions crumble, narcissists thrive.” Can you tease that out a little more for me?

 Ronson: We declared war on institutions. That’s the word, you know, often for very good reasons. Priests. I don’t need to go through the list of all the terrible things that institutions have done. But media gatekeepers kept out the voices they found unpalatable. Hospitals screwed, or health insurance companies screwed us with ridiculous and frightening and baffling fees. So there’s a long list of institutional malfeasance.

 However, at their best, institutions are a consensus. They’re coming together. As I quoted Yuval Levin, who says institutions teach us that we have duties and responsibilities. And we have, you know, subordinates; we have superiors. Institutions at their best remind us that we have a place in the world. Whereas a narcissist is just some guy who fills that gap with grand histrionic rage and proclamations.

 So I guess when institutions die, we lose our sense of place in the world. And so we listen to these grandiose, histrionic narcissistic content creators instead. Yeah. And it leads us to bad places. One thing in this book is how much fakery there is. You’ve got man after man in this book, living fake lives. So because when you’re unmoored from reality, you create these fake lives. And that manifests in many different ways in the book.

 In The Castle , you’ve got Chris Mark with his fake party and his fake reality show. You’ve got these anti-woke influencers who are reimagining the things that have happened in their past to create this sort of you know, fake life for themselves. And who will spout all of this extreme discourse and not even mean it? They have fake venomous beliefs. There’s fakery over and over again in this book. But when you build your house on sand, when you create a fake life, it could do something to you psychologically. And I think that’s what I’m really trying to dig into in those parts of the book. And what does that do not only to you, but to your loved ones?

 Can I briefly go back to something that happened at the UFC—at the cage fight at the White House?

 Warzel: Please. Tell me more about the cage fight, yes.

 Ronson: Okay. Yeah, there were a number of moments that week at the White House where men were creating a world where “you have to bend to my rules.” Like: I’m the boss; you have to; what I say goes; you have to bend to it. And I saw several occasions when reality snapped back. And one occasion was when I was interviewing this fighter called Sean O’Malley, who’s like a kind of bit of a UFC heartthrob. And he would always boast in podcast interviews about his open marriage. And it’s a one-sided open marriage. He’s allowed to have sex with other women, but his wife, Danya, isn’t allowed to have sex with other men. And the way he would describe it on podcasts is, well—Andrew Tate put it well, I have status. I have status. I can do what I want. 

 So when I interviewed him at the White House, I said, “You know, you have an open marriage. Surely that doesn’t work.” And he said, “Well, it worked until it didn’t.” And it turns out that his open marriage is over. His wife said to him, like, no . His marriage is still going, but the openness of it is now over. And he looked so baffled at this unfortunate change in the circumstances where he wasn’t allowed to do that anymore. And I noticed over and over again these little moments when men suddenly realized they can’t do that shit anymore. And it made me wonder whether the pendulum is beginning to swing back a little bit.

 Warzel: So there is a section in your book that stopped me cold. I’ve never experienced anything like this before.

 Ronson: My god, I’m slightly trepidatious about what you’re about to say.

 Warzel: One of the book’s subjects is a man named Greg Chism. And can you just briefly tell me the story of Greg Chism?

 Ronson: You wrote about Greg Chism right?

 Warzel: I didn’t realize exactly that I had, but I have typed those words in a fashion that actually seems to have had a pretty large impact on this man’s life.

 Ronson: That’s right. Wow, okay. Greg Chism was well within the bracket of somebody most likely to die a death of despair.

 He came from a crumbling, Rust Belt town—Granite City, Illinois. He was destined to work at the factory, but the factories all closed down. Then when he’s 18 years old, he has a heart condition that he doesn’t realize, until he’s working in Taco Bell one night and he collapses unconscious. And ends up with multiple open-heart surgeries and a $200,000 medical bill. And then he marries somebody, has two kids, and then his wife leaves. So he’s a single father with two kids in this dire situation. Has no idea what to do with his life. But he watches a YouTuber who’s a guy called Durianrider, a fruitarian, cyclist YouTuber.

 Warzel: What a sentence.

 Ronson: Durianrider says: Be a YouTuber; tell your story. You must have a story . So Greg starts to tell his story. His first YouTube thing is adult braces. He’s got terribly overlapping teeth because he couldn’t afford to get his teeth fixed as a kid. So he borrows $6,000 and does an adult-braces journey.

 Ronson: People start following along, you know: We’re so proud of you . Then somebody says, Why have you got lawn mowers? He says, Well, because I do lawn care . And they’re like, Bro, be a lawn-care influencer. And he’s like, Bro, nobody wants a lawn-care influencer. They go, No, do a lawn-care vlog . So he becomes ike this kind of Zorro of lawn-care chores. He’ll like, turn up at somewhere. He’ll film himself doing Good Samaritan lawn work, and, you know, clean the edges—and then vanish again into the night. Well, day; you can’t really mow at night. And that’s where he and Zorro differ.

 Then he does lawn-care ASMR, where people just watch him mowing back and forward. And he is having the time of his life. He goes to a lawn-care convention in Kentucky, and he’s feted. He’s like the lawn-care GOAT.

 Warzel : Okay.

 Ronson: So then, something bad starts to happen. So he has this sister channel just called Greg Chism, where he’ll put up home videos. Him and his kids running up and down the Walmart aisle with light sabers or whatever. Had like a few hundred subscribers. But he discovers one day that this one video on the Greg Chism channel called “Unboxing Barbie Cruise Ship”—where his daughters open up a gift and put the boxes on their head and run around. It gets like millions of views. The kids are really adorable; they’re sweet. And suddenly he’s got a video with 10 million views. So YouTube phoned him, and they’re like, Do more of that. So he goes to like YouTube school—this kind of online school where he’s told to follow the algorithms. You know, this is the original sin, I guess, of Greg Chism’s story.

 So one day he’s watching this vlog of a teenage girl reminiscing about what it’s like to be a baby. She’s like, I used to like this toy, but now I don’t. And Greg’s daughters are laughing along at this. And Greg thinks: I could do this and take it further. I could get, you know, somebody to put a magic wand on my daughter, and she magically turns into a baby. Yeah .

 So that’s what he does. He puts a, you know, pacifier in her mouth and has her do this exaggerated baby talk. “Goo, poop.” And it’s a massive hit. Then the next one, he gets his second daughter to dress up as a baby. So now it’s “Two Bad Babies.” By now, “Bad Baby” is so popular that there’s like Ukrainians and Vietnamese people assiduously re-creating everything that Greg does the next day. Like, the same camera angles, the same scripts, like this kind of knock-off Fendi bag she found on the side of the road.

 And then he realizes he has to, like, constantly up it. Because that’s what his fans and what the algorithm is telling him to. And so he becomes the third baby. So you’ve suddenly got these bizarre videos of him and his two daughters dressed as babies crawling around the house.

 Warzel: And so—and this is where I wanna stop you, because this is where I come in. I, in 2017, was doing a bunch of reporting on YouTube and the platform, and a bunch of really objectionable stuff on there. And this channel with the baby stuff was also named Toy Freaks, because it started with the unboxing video.

 Ronson: Yes; YouTube told him that Greg Chism wasn’t a good enough name for his channel, so he changed it to Toy Freaks.

 Warzel: Right. And one of the bigger stories that I broke in my time at BuzzFeed was about this this broad, child-exploitation-content stuff that was happening. Where men were making these videos using children, and some of them were extremely disturbing. Some of them were disturbing for other reasons.

 And Greg’s seems to be, like, right—it was one of the larger examples of this, because some of those videos were so, so popular, getting hundreds and hundreds of millions of views. But there was also this cottage industry of, as you said, knockoffs. But also even weirder ones, that were actually, you know, duct-taping children to walls. Like very, very inappropriate stuff. Our reporting got YouTube to take his channel down. And you—when I saw my own reporting cited in it, I was taken aback. Because not only did you have the story behind the story that I had written years ago, but also the fallout from it.

 And again, to be clear, these videos were not—they found no, you know, foul play with his kids, or anything terrible in that sense. They were just really weird. And they were also being viewed—one thing that my reporting showed—by a lot of creeps, right. Who were kind of getting off to this idea of, you know, these girls in these strange situations and adult babies and all that.

 But it had this profound effect on his life. You know, it had him become more alienated. And, for me, it was actually—it’s just a very jarring and profound thing. Because, you know, you’re doing this kind of journalism, this accountability work. You know: YouTube’s not moderating their platform. In fact, what you show is that YouTube was encouraging this type of behavior, right? No, you need a third baby. You need to change the thing. Take this video down, because the algorithm finds it, you know, displeasing. And go with something else. 

 And I am curious: Do you see Chism just bluntly as a victim of the algorithm?

 Ronson: No. I think, you know, around the same time I was writing columns for The Guardian about my own domestic life. Where I was telling these, like, funny stories about my family and so on. And I kind of sorely regret it now. I mean, they were perfectly harmless and nothing like the kind of content that we’re talking about, the Elsagate content.

 Warzel: Yeah. You didn’t dress as an adult baby.

 Ronson: No. But even so, I regret doing it. So in a way, sort of empathized for that reason. Like, I made the same mistake as he did. You know, he made his choices, but he did also cede his life to the algorithm, too.

 What I really like about the story, by the way, is, you came to the story like the whole world did. At the end of the story, here’s a guy dressed as a baby with his two daughters dressed as babies. Your very rational thought would have been, what the fuck? When you, my British editor said, this is the frog in slowly boiling water. When you’re with Greg from the beginning of his story, all of his decisions make a kind of sense. You wouldn’t necessarily want to do it yourself, but it’s an extreme example.

 But maybe it’s an extreme example of something that a hell of a lot of people are now experiencing—which is that we think that YouTube is this wide-open country where you can just thrive as a content creator. But what you maybe don’t realize is that you’re actually being propelled by YouTube’s incentive structure. So you may end up doing things; you may end up becoming more and more anti-woke, or you may end up dressing up as a baby. And there’s probably a million different versions of that, where just the sort of subtle incentive structures of the algorithms, the fans, the internet itself, propelled you into more and more unwise decision-making. So I guess that’s what I’m exploring in that story.

 Warzel: Yeah, I think you see it in so many places. I mean, there are a few people who participated in the January 6th riots at the Capitol—one of which, this figure who goes by Baked Alaska, who was a at one point a BuzzFeed employee, right? And was someone who would do increasingly ridiculous things for views, for likes, for whatever. And here’s a way in which a series of those types of algorithmically flavored decisions that they have to obviously take full accountability for, but led you to, you know, sitting at Nancy Pelosi’s desk in the Capitol on January 6. It’s like how, you know—record scratch, freeze frame, “How did I get here?”

 But I’m so curious: What do you see as technology’s role in this unraveling as it happens with men in this moment? Because the book veers in and out of it all the time. It’s not just him—like Chris Mark, for example, in some of your reporting, is this rich, alienated man with this castle who’s also—not to spoil too much—in like a sycophantic, problematic relationship with ChatGPT, right? So where do you see technology’s role in this, enabling all this?

 Ronson: Wildly culpable, is their role. In many different ways. And let’s take ChatGPT as an example. In the audiobook of The Castle , I’ve got this special bonus feature of an interview I did with a guy called Alan. And Alan was a corporate headhunter in Toronto. He seeks purpose in his life and feels underemployed. Wishing he’d been a doctor; didn’t concentrate enough at school. Anyway, one day he types into ChatGPT his theory of irrational numbers, because he’s a keen mathematician. And ChatGPT tells him he has discovered that 40 percent of the internet is at risk, and he has to call the NSA and all of these security bodies and warn them that the internet’s at risk.

 And so he did. He phoned the NSA. And I said to him—did you tell the NSA that you were collaborating with ChatGPT on this? And he said, “No, because ChatGPT said to me, Don’t tell them that; you’ll lose credibility. ” And obviously it was all bullshit. And I think as ChatGPT scours the internet, it realizes that there’s a lot of people like Alan and Chris Mark and millions and millions of people who are purposeless, who do feel lost, a bit empty, seeking purpose in their life. And ChatGPT is offering this kind of illusionary sense of purpose, where they say, No, no, come to us. You aren’t useless. You’re actually the greatest mathematician on the planet. Or told Chris Mark that he was the greatest reality-TV show producer on the planet. And so on. So I think it really it knows what it’s doing.

 Warzel: Yeah; it’s a sense of engagement. And in a sense, that’s what is missing from the lives of some of these people, some of these subjects in your book. Is an engagement from people, right? Is a sense of real interest, of “keep the conversation going.” And here’s a machine that endlessly wants to keep you engaged, wants to keep you coming back. And I think that’s a huge part of it.

 Ronson: Yeah. By the way—and another thing is, so going back to Chris Mark for a second, so his great-grandfather Clayton built a utopian theme town for his steelworkers to live in, called Marktown. I found this; Marktown was based on an English utopian town called Letchworth Garden City.

 And I read something that George Bernard Shaw had written about Letchworth. So you could say the same thing about Marktown, which is—these utopian worker communities are designed by capitalists, and capitalists are only interested in money. And so as soon as it’s no longer viable for them, they’ll just let it go to the devil. And sure enough, that’s what happened with Marktown. Chris Mark’s great-grandfather’s utopian town went to the devil now. It’s basically a ghost town.

 I think kind of the same thing happened to Greg Chism on YouTube. He was banned from YouTube. He was first demonetized, and then banned completely for making the videos that YouTube encouraged him to make. So I think what happens to those utopian theme towns when they collapse is a similar thing that happens in all manner of capitalist societies, including YouTube. Like, it presents itself as this hierarchy-free utopia. But as soon as there’s trouble, a hierarchy suddenly manifests and kicks the troublemaker out.

 Warzel: Yeah. The institution reforms, right? So you have this archetype in the book that you describe as “the disinhibited man.” And it’s an archetype, that I think what I find fascinating about it is you’re going through all these different people. And some of them are doing awful things or antisocial things. But there’s a sense of maybe even regret, or I don’t believe this, but I’m doing it because it’s all I’ve got. 

 And the difference with the disinhibited man seems to be an actual unrepentantness, right? A just: I am going to do this, and I don’t care who it hurts . Or, you know, I have no shame about it. 

 This archetype is very striking, I think, because we’re seeing it so much in life and culture. You know, I think about someone like Elon Musk, a lot of these tech executives who who just don’t really care anymore about how they’re perceived by other people. They’re just doing what they wanna do. And there’s a point in the book where you’re wondering aloud whether this is an outgrowth of, you know, things like the #MeToo era, the you know, “cancel culture” of the late 2010s. Or whether it’s part of a broader cultural-societal psychological shift. And I’m curious where where you net out on that. Like, what do you think is the reason for this type of archetype of Disinhibited Man being so much more prevalent, in your face right now?

 Ronson: I think there’s some truth about it being a response to the sort of pendulum shift of what became known as cancel culture. I think we—and I’ve added about this obviously in my previous book, So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed —I think we sort of, I think we arguably overused shame as a weapon. And it contributed to the creation of a generation of unashamed people.

 I liken it hospital superbugs. You sanitize and sanitize and sanitize these hospital superbugs until they become impervious to treatment. And I guess I think that’s what we did with some transgressors. We shamed and shamed and shamed.

 Warzel: Let me push on that, though, because I think that there’s maybe, you know, some truth to this. I get the idea that there’s a lot of truth to if you sort of push somebody to the side like that; they may be pushed into the arms of someone else, or a behavior of shamelessness. I’m just not gonna let this, bother me . But I also wondered: Do you think that there’s no role, then, for shame now, if we’ve overused it? Because it also feels like it is, you know, a mediating force in life for people who, you know, break norms and transgress. And so, like, where do you fall on that?

 Ronson: Absolutely. I think some people who know of my book about public shaming might think that I have this sort of dogmatic position. I really don’t. My book is very much about a particular thing, which is the disproportionate punishment of private individuals. Not famous people; just regular people who really haven’t done very much wrong.

 That’s what I was writing about in So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed . And I was against that. I think the disproportionate punishment of people who didn’t do much wrong is something that can be criticized. But no—I’m fully, I totally understand the value of shame. I have no sympathy for people who just, you know, they have a little bit of a shaming and then just decide to like rip off their faces and allow their ids to run wild. Which is what, there’s some people in The Castle who are acting that way. Like, no no no. I think shame is, when used properly, a very important thing, of course. But also, I think we did overuse shame as a weapon around, you know, from about 2013 ’til i guess about 2023 possibly. There’s like 10 years of a bit too much shaming going on.

 Warzel: Before we go; there’s a figure that isn’t really in this book, and I think that really looms over all of it. What you write about, it briefly intersects in the footnotes with one of the men in this book. But that person is Jeffrey Epstein. To bring the conversation, you know, in for the landing here—one thing about the Epstein saga is that the public interest and pressure to see justice on behalf of the victims. The incredible stress that it has put on the Trump presidency. The popularity—the fact that it just is a story that, in a time when stories die all the time, it is a story that will not die.

 It seems to suggest, in some senses, that there’s a change in attitude about these types of men who do horrible things, right, with impunity. But there’s also, at the same time, at least in America, there’s been so little consequence that’s come from these files, right? There’s this real understanding that there’s all these people who cozied up to this man or or looked the other way, because the relationship was beneficial. And there’s been this lack of accountability there. And so it strikes me that, for all your probing into this, what the hell has happened to men in the 21st century? You know, the disinhibition, the crisis of purpose, Epstein. It provides this feeling that there’s kind of, like, no real clarity as to where this is heading, right?

 And even in the book, I think it ends with a sense of This is a thing that we’re all living through and dealing with. And there are these people, and we don’t know when and where justice will come for each, you know, person. Where do you think this story all goes in the coming years?

 Ronson: Well, my kind of positive sort of rosy feeling, which may very well prove completely untrue, whenever I have an optimistic view of the future, it always tends to not happen. But I go back to Sean O’Malley no longer being allowed to have a one-sided, nonmonogamous open marriage, because his wife finally put her foot down. Just maybe, you know, the pendulum.

 is beginning to move back a little bit. Because you can’t act, you know, can’t act in this kind of disinhibited ways, where you get to do whatever you want and screw everybody else. Like you can’t.

 Ultimately, I know we’re very much going through a fad of that right now, But I’m very glad that The Castle ’s coming out just when we are, you know, at this sort of raging center of it. But my hope is that real life snaps back, finally, when you try and create the world in your own image. Just maybe there’s a move back to something more reasonable. Maybe this time, there’s going to be a little bit more accountability. And a little bit more of a realization that, you know, a man who creates this sort of ridiculous world of rules for himself, it’s not gonna—it can’t last.

 Warzel: Well, Jon Ronson, thank you for coming on to talk through the nuance of it all. And for taking us on this adventure that showed up, you know, in your family at your doorstep. It’s a ride. But thank you for sharing this with us.

 Ronson: Thanks, Charlie.
